title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 01–02
description: Advanced study skills, academic writing, education policy and educational opportunity, with emphasis on register, collocations and semantic contrasts.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study based on a user-provided book. Vocabulary targets and uses are grounded in the source units, exercises and answer key; translations, definitions, original sample sentences and usage notes were freshly written, without reproducing exercises, long passages or source illustrations.

audit.scope: Unit 1 and Unit 2 teaching sections, definitions, Language help, exercises 1.1–1.4 and 2.1–2.4, and the corresponding answer key.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is supplied for relatively short targets where confident. Blank IPA means that a reliable entry-level transcription has not been established; it is not an indication that the expression is silent. IPA does not attempt full connected-speech transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: All learner-facing explanations, examples and metadata are in English; Portuguese appears only in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Teaching and exercise pages, academic-writing distinctions and the answer key were compared; examples were written independently. JSON syntax, schema parity, IDs, item text, audio fields and TTS target handling were checked programmatically. Browser import and speech recognition were not tested.
audit.limitations: This JSON contains no recorded MP3 audio. Browser-dependent TTS and pronunciation recognition require testing in VocabLab. The academic qualification and educational-system terms follow the book’s predominantly British-English context and may differ by institution or country.

units.title: Unit 01 — Cramming for success: study and academic work
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 1. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Work and study · study strategies and academic writing
learningObjectives: Distinguish cramming, revision, memorisation, rote-learning and effective use of mnemonics.
Select composition, essay, assignment, project, portfolio, dissertation or thesis for different written tasks.
Use academic-integrity and submission expressions, including plagiarism, acknowledge a source, submit and assess.
Discuss academic journals, research papers, inter-library loans and open educational resources with natural collocations.

sectionsChecked: A and B teaching sections, definitions and annotated vocabulary

items.pt: estudar intensamente na última hora para uma prova
items.example: She had to cram for the chemistry exam after missing several classes.
items.note: Cramming usually happens shortly before an exam; it contrasts with sustained revision.

items.example: A night of cramming left him exhausted before the test.
items.note: Noun referring to intensive last-minute exam study.

items.example: Her colleagues consider her a genius at solving complex problems.
items.note: A highly intelligent or exceptionally talented person; the plural is geniuses.

items.pt: revisão para prova; estudo de revisão
items.example: I schedule revision throughout the semester instead of waiting until the final week.
items.note: In British English, revision commonly means reviewing material for an exam.

items.example: They revise for their exams in the library every afternoon.
items.note: British English revise for an exam means study material again; US English often uses review.

items.example: Practising with past papers helped her understand the exam format.
items.note: Papers here means examination papers, not academic research articles.

items.example: It is easier to memorise definitions when you understand the concepts first.
items.note: British spelling; American English usually memorizes.

items.example: He learned the opening paragraph by heart before the presentation.
items.note: An idiom meaning memorise something exactly; something represents the object to be learnt.

items.example: Rote-learning may help with basic facts but cannot replace critical thinking.
items.note: Refers to learning through repetition, sometimes without understanding.

items.pt: técnicas mnemônicas; recursos para ajudar a memória
items.example: She uses mnemonics to remember the order of the planets.
items.note: Plural noun; the initial m is silent, and stress falls on the second syllable.

items.example: The phrase became a useful mnemonic for recalling the formula.
items.note: Singular form of mnemonics; may be a word, phrase, image or other memory aid.

items.pt: considerando tudo; levando tudo em conta
items.example: All things considered, the course offered good value for money.
items.note: A discourse expression introducing an overall judgement after weighing different factors.

items.pt: mergulhar nos estudos; dedicar-se intensamente aos livros
items.example: She buried herself in her books for several weeks before the qualifying exam.
items.note: Figurative expression meaning spend a great deal of time studying.

items.example: The students studied intensively during the final month of the programme.
items.note: Intensively describes concentrated effort, not merely studying often.

items.example: She worked intensively on her research proposal throughout July.
items.note: An adverb meaning with concentrated effort and attention.

items.pt: dominar completamente um assunto; conhecer de ponta a ponta
items.example: After years of practice, the lecturer knows the subject inside out.
items.note: Know something inside out means be thoroughly familiar with it.

items.example: The teacher asked the children to write a short composition about their neighbourhood.
items.note: In the unit, composition is a relatively short school writing task; not the same as a PhD thesis.

items.example: For the history module, we wrote an essay comparing two political systems.
items.note: Generally longer and more analytical than a short school composition.

items.example: The assignment is due next Friday and counts towards the final mark.
items.note: A piece of work assigned as part of a course; the book contrasts its scale with a short essay.

items.pt: projeto acadêmico; trabalho com pesquisa própria
items.example: Their project involved interviewing local residents and analysing the responses.
items.note: The book emphasises a learner's independent topic or materials.

items.example: She submitted a portfolio containing reports, designs and reflections.
items.note: A collection of separate pieces of work, rather than one continuous essay.

items.pt: dissertação acadêmica; trabalho de pesquisa para obtenção de título
items.example: His master's dissertation examines how online communities share knowledge.
items.note: In the book's UK-oriented comparison, a substantial research work for a degree or diploma; naming varies between institutions.

items.pt: tese; pesquisa acadêmica extensa e original
items.example: She defended her doctoral thesis after four years of research.
items.note: In the unit, associated with an extensive research work for a higher degree such as a PhD; plural theses.

items.example: He created a mind map before organising the chapters of his report.
items.note: A diagram that shows how ideas and concepts relate to each other.

items.example: The supervisor suggested major changes to the first draft of the introduction.
items.note: Draft means a provisional version, not the finished document.

items.example: Her draft still needs a clearer conclusion and better references.
items.note: As a noun, a preliminary version; also a verb meaning prepare an initial text.

items.pt: redigir ou passar a limpo resultados; preparar versão escrita definitiva
items.example: After collecting the data, the team wrote up its findings for publication.
items.note: Write up findings or an essay means prepare a finished written account; a separable phrasal verb.

items.example: Check all the citations before sending the final version to the examiner.
items.note: The completed version after editing and revision.

items.example: The declaration confirms that the report is all your own work.
items.note: Academic-integrity expression: it must be your independent work, with external contributions acknowledged.

items.example: The committee investigated an allegation of plagiarism in the submitted report.
items.note: Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without appropriate acknowledgement.

items.example: Falsifying results is considered a serious offence at the university.
items.note: Offence in this context means a serious violation of rules or standards.

items.pt: recortar e colar; copiar e colar conteúdo
items.example: Simply cutting and pasting online material is not an acceptable research method.
items.note: The expression describes moving or copying material between documents; it does not by itself imply plagiarism.

items.pt: declaração de autoria e ausência de plágio
items.example: Every student signed a plagiarism form when submitting the final report.
items.note: A form used to confirm academic-integrity requirements; terminology varies by institution.

items.pt: entregar; apresentar um trabalho para avaliação
items.example: Students must hand in their lab reports by noon.
items.note: Common, less formal alternative to submit in academic contexts.

items.pt: citar ou reconhecer uma fonte utilizada
items.example: Always acknowledge a source when you quote an author's research.
items.note: Acknowledge means give appropriate credit; different from merely referring casually to someone.

items.example: The author acknowledged the researchers whose data she had used.
items.note: In academic writing, formally identify a contribution or source.

items.example: The application deadline is two weeks earlier than I expected.
items.note: A time or date by which something must be completed or submitted.

items.example: Please submit the revised manuscript through the university portal.
items.note: More formal than hand in when referring to assignments, manuscripts or applications.

items.example: Two independent lecturers will assess each research proposal.
items.note: In education, assess means evaluate the quality or achievement of a piece of work.

items.pt: comentários de avaliação; retorno sobre desempenho
items.example: Detailed feedback helped her improve the argument in the next draft.
items.note: Feedback is usually uncountable: receive some feedback, not receive a feedback.

items.pt: receber comentários de avaliação; obter retorno
items.example: You can get feedback on your essay before submitting the final version.
items.note: Common combination: get or receive feedback on something.

items.example: A university academic was invited to review the new curriculum.
items.note: Academic as a countable noun means a scholar or university teaching/research professional.

items.example: The laboratory carries out research into low-power electronic devices.
items.note: A more formal collocation than do research; research is uncountable in this meaning.

items.example: Their research focuses on real-time systems.
items.note: Normally uncountable: some research, not a research, in this sense.

items.example: The results were published in a peer-reviewed academic journal.
items.note: A journal contains scholarly articles; the book says not to use magazine for this kind of publication.

items.example: She published a paper on sensor calibration methods.
items.note: In research, paper can mean a scholarly article; past papers in Section A are old exam papers.

items.example: The article summarises several approaches to data analysis.
items.note: May refer to a research publication in a journal; not exclusively a newspaper article.

items.pt: assunto especializado; tema de área específica
items.example: The journal accepts papers on highly specialised subjects.
items.note: British spelling specialised; restricted to a particular field or discipline.

items.example: The research group can access the journal online through its library.
items.note: Access is transitive here: access a journal, not access to a journal as a verb phrase.

items.example: The librarian arranged an inter-library loan for a rare reference book.
items.note: A library obtains material from another library for a reader.

items.example: Open educational resources make course materials available beyond the university.
items.note: Often abbreviated OER; the unit describes resources that can be freely used by educators and students.

items.example: Completing the research programme was intellectually demanding.
items.note: Describes something requiring a great deal of work, skill or effort.

items.pt: abandonar um curso antes de concluí-lo
items.example: Some learners drop out because they cannot combine study with full-time work.
items.note: In academic contexts, drop out of a course means leave before completion.

items.pt: exames finais de um curso; provas finais
items.example: She spent most of May preparing for her finals.
items.note: The book uses finals for examinations at the end of a degree course.

items.example: The employer is looking for well-qualified applicants with research experience.
items.note: Means having the appropriate qualifications; hyphenated before a noun.

items.example: Applicants must demonstrate their formal qualifications before enrolment.
items.note: The book refers to having the right formal qualifications to enter a profession.

units.title: Unit 02 — Education: debates and issues
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 2. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Work and study · education policy, opportunity and inequality
learningObjectives: Discuss equality of opportunity, selective versus comprehensive education and two-tier systems.
Differentiate scholarships from bursaries, student loans, tuition fees and living expenses.
Compare undergraduate, postgraduate and tertiary education terminology.
Discuss curriculum reform, literacy, numeracy, mature students and inclusive educational provision.
Use compound adjectives and formal collocations to discuss inequalities and educational performance.

sectionsChecked: A and B teaching sections, definitions and annotated vocabulary
Language help box and terminology contrasts

items.example: The policy aims to improve equality of opportunity across the school system.
items.note: Having a fair chance to succeed, regardless of background or circumstances.

items.pt: educação com seleção de alunos por critérios de ingresso
items.example: Selective education admits pupils according to specified admission criteria.
items.note: In this unit, selection is usually based on ability or examination results; some private-school admission also reflects fees.

items.pt: educação abrangente com ingresso não seletivo
items.example: Supporters of comprehensive education argue that children should learn together.
items.note: In the unit's British context, this model does not select pupils through academic entry tests.

items.example: She received most of her schooling in a small town.
items.note: Education received at school; differs from tertiary education.

items.example: Family income should not determine educational achievement.
items.note: Success or attainment in education, often measured through assessments.

items.example: Critics argued that the admissions policy encouraged elitism.
items.note: Favouring or privileging a small, supposedly superior group.

items.example: Some researchers argue that these inequalities are inherent in the system.
items.note: The unit uses the pattern inherent in something for a basic, built-in quality.

items.pt: rankings comparativos de escolas ou instituições
items.example: Parents sometimes rely too heavily on league tables when choosing schools.
items.note: Ranked lists of schools or colleges based on performance measures; UK educational usage.

items.example: An unfair policy can perpetuate social disadvantage.
items.note: A relatively formal verb meaning cause something, often harmful, to continue.

items.example: The report argues that unequal resources perpetuate inequalities.
items.note: A useful academic collocation expressing the continuation of inequality.

items.pt: elevar padrões de qualidade; melhorar níveis de desempenho
items.example: The reform was designed to raise standards in public education.
items.note: Raise standards means improve quality, not simply increase the number of requirements.

items.example: The educational institution introduced a new accessibility policy.
items.note: Includes schools, colleges and universities in this context.

items.pt: sistema de dois níveis; sistema de categorias desiguais
items.example: Critics feared the changes would create a two-tier system of healthcare and education.
items.note: Refers to a system with two levels, one advantaged relative to the other.

items.example: Parents may perceive the policy as unfair even when the official criteria are clear.
items.note: More formal than see when it means interpret or consider something.

items.pt: em melhor situação financeira; mais abastado
items.example: Better-off families can often pay for additional tutoring.
items.note: Comparative form associated with well-off; describes relative financial advantage.

items.pt: bem financiado; dotado de recursos financeiros abundantes
items.example: The well-endowed university provides generous research grants.
items.note: Financially endowed in this context; not a description of a person's appearance.

items.pt: fundo patrimonial; doação para financiamento institucional
items.example: The college used income from its endowment to fund scholarships.
items.note: Money or assets donated and held to support an institution; connected with well-endowed.

items.example: A poorly designed admissions policy can depress opportunities for disadvantaged pupils.
items.note: Depress can formally mean lower or reduce; not necessarily describe a feeling.

items.pt: menos favorecido financeiramente; com menos recursos
items.example: The scheme provides support for students from less well-off households.
items.note: Comparative expression describing relative economic disadvantage.

items.example: She excelled in mathematics despite having limited resources.
items.note: Typically excel at or in something; not the same as bullying.

items.pt: bolsa de estudos por mérito acadêmico
items.example: Her high grades helped her win a scholarship to study physics.
items.note: The book associates scholarship with academic merit; actual eligibility rules vary.

items.pt: bolsa ou auxílio estudantil baseado em necessidade financeira
items.example: The bursary covered his travel and accommodation costs.
items.note: In the book, bursaries are typically based on financial need; institutions may use the term differently.

items.example: More young people now have access to tertiary education.
items.note: Education at university or college level; follows secondary education.

items.example: She took out a student loan to cover living costs during her degree.
items.note: Borrowed money that normally must be repaid under the loan terms.

items.example: As an undergraduate, he worked part-time in the university library.
items.note: A student studying for a first degree; contrast postgraduate.

items.example: The postgraduate is conducting research for a master's degree.
items.note: Studies for a degree or qualification after a first degree.

items.pt: mensalidades ou taxas cobradas pelo ensino
items.example: The university published updated tuition fees for international students.
items.note: Fees paid for teaching, typically at a university or college.

items.pt: despesas de manutenção; custos de vida
items.example: Her grant covered only part of her living expenses.
items.note: Costs of accommodation, food, transport and other everyday needs.

items.example: The programme offers mentoring to learners from less privileged backgrounds.
items.note: Refers to people with fewer social or material advantages.

items.example: Applicants are considered on the basis of academic merit.
items.note: Achievement or excellence in study, used as a basis for some scholarships.

items.example: The foundation provides financial support for students with limited income.
items.note: A broad expression encompassing grants, bursaries and other assistance.

items.pt: os três fundamentos: leitura, escrita e aritmética
items.example: The education minister called for renewed attention to the three Rs.
items.note: Traditional phrase for reading, writing and arithmetic; only reading begins with R literally.

items.example: Adult literacy programmes can improve access to employment.
items.note: In the book's contrast, literacy concerns reading, while numeracy concerns numbers.

items.pt: competência matemática básica; capacidade de lidar com números
items.example: The course includes activities designed to develop numeracy.
items.note: Ability to work with numbers and basic mathematics, not reading skills.

items.example: Curriculum reform can change what students learn at every stage of school.
items.note: Changes to the subjects, content or structure of a curriculum.

items.pt: programa de estudos; ementa de conteúdo
items.example: The updated syllabus includes digital literacy and statistics.
items.note: A plan of topics to be studied; curriculum is generally broader than one course's syllabus.

items.pt: educação ao longo da vida; aprendizagem contínua
items.example: Lifelong education allows adults to retrain throughout their careers.
items.note: Learning opportunities extending across adulthood, not just childhood and university.

items.example: The college offers continuing education courses for working adults.
items.note: In this unit, a close alternative to lifelong education; often refers to organised adult courses.

items.pt: estudante adulto; aluno mais velho do que a média
items.example: As a mature student, she returned to university after ten years at work.
items.note: British education term for someone entering study at an older-than-typical age.

items.pt: educação para estudantes com necessidades educacionais específicas
items.example: Schools need trained staff and suitable resources for special needs education.
items.note: The unit uses this term for additional educational support; terminology and policy vary by country.

items.pt: ensino individualizado; aula particular entre professor e aluno
items.example: The tutor arranged one-to-one teaching for students who needed extra help.
items.note: One teacher works with one student rather than a whole class.

items.example: The school introduced measures to prevent bullying during breaks.
items.note: Repeated threatening or intimidating behaviour; not the same as excelling.

items.example: The headteacher met parents to discuss the school's new policy.
items.note: British English term for the person who leads a school.

items.pt: compreender e aprender a lidar com algo difícil
items.example: New staff needed time to get to grips with the updated assessment rules.
items.note: Means begin to understand and handle a complex matter successfully.

items.example: Schools received new government guidelines on safeguarding.
items.note: Guidelines are recommendations or instructions on how something should be done.

items.example: The guideline explains how to report an absence.
items.note: General direction or advice; not the same as a ranking or league table.

items.pt: distração; fator que desvia a atenção
items.example: Frequent administrative interruptions can become a distraction from teaching.
items.note: A person or thing that takes attention away from an important task.

items.example: The policy puts emphasis on early reading skills.
items.note: Pattern emphasis on something; often put or place emphasis on.

items.example: The town has both well-off and low-income neighbourhoods.
items.note: Base adjective referring to financial comfort; compare better-off and less well-off.

items.pt: de alto desempenho; com excelentes resultados
items.example: High-achieving pupils also benefit from challenging lessons.
items.note: Compound adjective often used for students or schools with strong results.

items.pt: de baixo desempenho; com resultados ruins
items.example: The new policy offered support to badly-performing schools.
items.note: Compound adjective for something that performs poorly; one comparison is worst-performing.

items.example: Higher-achieving groups were assigned additional enrichment activities.
items.note: Comparative of high-achieving as highlighted in the book's Language help box.

items.example: The inspectorate provided extra support to the worst-performing schools.
items.note: Superlative of badly-performing, as contrasted in the Language help box.

items.pt: ensino primário; primeiros anos da educação escolar
items.example: Primary education gives children foundations in reading and arithmetic.
items.note: Precedes secondary education; appears explicitly in Exercise 2.3.

items.pt: ensino secundário; etapa escolar anterior ao ensino superior
items.example: She completed secondary education before applying to college.
items.note: Follows primary education and precedes tertiary education in the book's distinction.

items.pt: mensalidades escolares; taxas cobradas por escolas
items.example: Some private schools charge school fees, while state schools are publicly funded.
items.note: Fees charged for school attendance; different context from university tuition fees.
